1Dialogue: Family lunch
MayaAt the café last weekend, Grandma kept asking us to say things again because of the noise. That’s why I’d rather have lunch here on Saturday.
AdamYes. I can collect her, but I have to leave again at two.
MayaShe has offered to help us make the salad.
AdamGood. Let’s ask which ingredients she’d like in it.
What was Maya's main reason for suggesting lunch at home?
A. Grandma had difficulty following the family's conversation.
B. Grandma had offered to help prepare part of the family's meal.
C. Adam had limited time to spend with the family that afternoon.
Review Answer
Answer: A
Grandma had trouble following the family conversation at the cafe. Maya links that experience to eating at home; cooking and Adam's departure time are separate details.
2Family Walking Challenge
For the next four weeks, choose three days each week for a family walk. The days may change from week to week. Every recorded walk must start and finish at home, and at least two family members must take part together. Keep one record for your family. Extra walks on your own are welcome, but they cannot be included in the family total. We will recognise families who keep going regularly, rather than those who cover the greatest distance.
Which walk can be included in the family record?
A. A teenager walks the usual route alone to make up for missing a family walk.
B. Two relatives walk from home and back together on their newly chosen day.
C. A family walks home from a nearby park after getting a lift there.
Review Answer
Answer: B
The walk starts and finishes at home with two family members. The family may change the walking days.
3Email: Dinner on Friday
From: Hana To: Amir
Subject: Dinner on Friday

Dad has to work late, so our family dinner will start at eight instead of seven. Mum says you are still welcome to come earlier. We could prepare the salad while we wait, but she has already bought everything we need. Please don’t bring the cake you mentioned: my sister is practising baking and wants us to try hers. If the later finish is a problem, Dad can drive you home afterwards.
Which reply shows that Amir has understood the arrangements?
A. “I’ll come at eight with the salad ingredients, then try your sister’s cake.”
B. “I’ll come at seven for dinner, then accept your dad’s lift home.”
C. “I’ll come at seven to help, then stay for dinner at eight.”
Review Answer
Answer: C
Amir may arrive early to help, but dinner begins at eight. The salad ingredients have already been bought.
4Café Review | The Green Spoon
The Green Spoon serves a small menu, but the dishes change with the vegetables available locally. My vegetable noodles were delicious, and the staff explained which dishes contained nuts. The room was noisy when we arrived, although it became quieter after the office workers left. We waited twenty minutes for our food. I would return with friends for a relaxed lunch, but I would choose somewhere else if I had only half an hour to eat.
Which conclusion is supported by the review?
A. Returning customers may find that a dish they enjoyed is no longer available.
B. Customers who avoid nuts can have their chosen dish prepared without them.
C. Customers arriving after the office workers leave can expect their food to come sooner.
Review Answer
Answer: A
Dishes vary with the vegetables available locally. The review does not establish that recipes can be adapted or that service becomes faster after the office workers leave.

5A Note from Mum
Leo, your cousin will stay in your room this weekend. Please move the books off the spare bed, but leave your school project on the desk: I know it isn’t finished. You don’t need to put all your things away. He is interested in model-making too, so you might enjoy showing him your work. I have washed the extra sheets and left them outside your door. Please make the bed before we collect him at five.
Thanks, Mum.
Why does Mum suggest leaving Leo's unfinished project on the desk?
A. It could help his cousin complete a similar school assignment.
B. It could give the boys something they both enjoy discussing.
C. It could encourage Leo to finish it before his cousin arrives.
Review Answer
Answer: B
The cousins share an interest in model-making. Nothing says the cousin needs assignment help or that Leo must finish the project before the visit.
6Community Cooking Afternoon
Saturday, 2–4 p.m. at Riverside Hall.
Learn to prepare two simple meals with a family member. Each pair pays RM12, which covers ingredients and equipment. You must book as a pair, but only one person needs previous cooking experience. Children under twelve must come with an adult. Bring a container to take your food home. Places are limited, so payment is required when booking. We cannot accept people who arrive without a booking, even if they bring their own ingredients.
Each pair plans to book and pay in advance. Which pair meets the other conditions for attending?
A. An eleven-year-old who often cooks and her sixteen-year-old cousin, who is a beginner.
B. A thirteen-year-old beginner and his nineteen-year-old brother, who is also a beginner.
C. A fifteen-year-old beginner and her seventeen-year-old sister, who often cooks.
Review Answer
Answer: C
Both sisters are at least twelve and one has cooking experience. A lacks an adult for the eleven-year-old; B has no experienced cook. All pairs book and pay in advance.
7Shopping Memo — Ella and Ben
Buy one packet of pasta and four small tomatoes. We already have mushrooms and cheese at home. The four tomatoes will make enough sauce only if all the mushrooms are cooked into it. Ben’s little brother would like his portion without cheese, so let everyone add their own after the pasta has been served.
Which plan follows all the instructions?
A. Buy the pasta and tomatoes; make tomato sauce, serve the mushrooms as a side dish and offer cheese separately.
B. Buy the pasta and tomatoes; cook the mushrooms in the sauce and offer cheese separately once everyone has a portion.
C. Buy the pasta and tomatoes; cook the mushrooms in the sauce and stir in cheese before dividing the meal.
Review Answer
Answer: B
All the mushrooms must be cooked into the sauce to make enough. Cheese remains separate so Ben’s brother can have a portion without it.
8Sam to Nina: Sunday Food Stall
I can arrive an hour before opening, but I must leave before closing to visit Grandpa. Your dad asked me to serve customers. Could I pack the orders first? I am still learning the dish names. After watching you, I could try serving. Arriving early should give me time to learn the routine.
How does Sam intend to prepare for the job Nina's dad has given him?
A. Learn the routine through another task, then move on to serving.
B. Learn the dishes before opening, then spend the shift packing.
C. Practise serving before opening, then let Nina take over the orders.
Review Answer
Answer: A
Sam proposes packing and watching Nina first, before trying to serve customers.

12Sunday Diary
I used to avoid my uncle’s restaurant because I thought every dish would be unfamiliar. Last Sunday, he suggested a sharing plate with small portions of several dishes. I recognised some ingredients, and he explained the others without making me feel foolish. I didn’t enjoy everything, but I discovered a bean dish I would order again. The experience showed me that trying something new doesn’t mean having to like all of it. Next time, I will bring a friend.
Why did the sharing plate help the writer change their view of the restaurant?

B. It helped the writer compare several dishes before recommending a meal to a friend.

Sampling several dishes led the writer to discover a bean dish worth ordering again.

Reading Part 3 · A Better Start to the School Day

Complete the fact file with no more than three words and/or a number from the text. Tap Review Answer to highlight matching evidence.

A Better Start to the School Day

When teenagers at Brookfield School were asked about their eating habits, several admitted that they often missed breakfast. Some said they were not hungry early in the morning, while others had little time before leaving home. The school's Healthy Living Club decided to investigate before suggesting a solution.

For three weeks, members asked pupils to complete a short daily record. They noted whether they had eaten breakfast and how they felt during the first lesson. The club did not ask anyone to record their weight or share private medical information. Its aim was to understand routines, not to judge pupils' bodies.

The records showed that lack of time was the main reason for missing breakfast. Buying food on the way to school was not a reliable solution because queues at nearby shops could be long. The club therefore proposed a small breakfast corner in the school canteen. The headteacher approved a trial lasting four weeks, provided that no lessons were interrupted.

The corner opened at 7.10 a.m. and closed twenty minutes later. Pupils could choose a banana, a boiled egg or a small bowl of porridge. Water was available too. The club deliberately avoided a large menu, which would have taken longer to prepare. Local shops donated some ingredients, while the parent association paid for the remaining supplies.

Volunteers worked in pairs. One served food while the other recorded the number of portions taken. They wore clean aprons and washed their hands before handling anything. To reduce waste, they prepared fewer portions at first and increased the amount only when demand became clearer. Pupils brought reusable containers if they wanted to take food to the outdoor eating area.

At the end of the trial, the club collected feedback. Most users said the corner helped them arrive at their first lesson feeling more comfortable. However, pupils travelling on the late bus could rarely use it. The club responded by setting aside a small number of portions until 7.40 a.m. for those pupils, who still had time to eat before lessons began.

The club will continue the project next term. Rather than claiming that one small change solves every problem, members plan to check the records each month and adjust the service when necessary. Their next task is to train more volunteers so that the same pupils do not have to work every morning.

Comprehension · Questions 53–62

Reading Part 4 · More Than a Table

Use no more than five words and/or a number. For Questions 61–62, find one word. Tap Review Answer to highlight the evidence.

More Than a Table

When fifteen-year-old Amir heard that his grandparents were selling their old dining table, he was more upset than he expected. The table was scratched, one leg was uneven, and his grandmother said it took up too much space. Yet Amir remembered birthdays, family arguments and long Sunday lunches around it. To him, it was more than a piece of furniture.

His first idea was to persuade his grandparents to keep it. His grandfather listened, then explained that they needed a smaller table because moving around the room had become difficult. Amir realised that his wish to keep a memory should not make their daily lives harder. Instead, he asked whether he could record some of the stories connected with the table before it went to its new owner.

At first, Amir planned to interview everyone at the same time. However, his aunt warned him that the louder relatives might dominate the conversation. He changed his plan and spoke to family members in pairs. He prepared a few questions, but he also allowed people to follow their own memories. Often, an unexpected detail led to the most interesting story.

His grandmother recalled a meal she had cooked during a power cut. His uncle remembered breaking a plate and trying to hide the pieces. Amir's mother described how the family had welcomed a neighbour who was spending a festival alone. Some stories were funny, while others made the speakers pause before continuing.

The recordings were not always easy to understand. Traffic outside the house covered parts of his grandfather's voice. Rather than inventing missing details, Amir played back the unclear sections and asked him to explain them again. He also discovered that two relatives remembered the same birthday differently. In his booklet, he included both accounts instead of deciding that one person must be wrong.

Amir added photographs of the table, close-ups of its marks and a simple family tree. He asked each person to check the pages about them before making copies. One aunt preferred to remove a personal story, and he respected her choice. The booklet was meant to bring the family together, not to make anyone uncomfortable.

On the day the table was collected, Amir felt sad, but he no longer thought that keeping it was the only way to protect the past. His grandparents placed the booklet on their new, smaller table. During lunch, they opened it and began telling stories that Amir had not heard before. He took out his notebook. The project, he realised, was not finished simply because the old table had left the house.

Gapped Text · Questions 63–68

Reading Part 5 · The Recipe That Changed

Tap each numbered gap to display options A–H. Tap an option for Correct or Wrong — try again. The explanation appears only after a correct choice; there are two extra sentences.

The Recipe That Changed

Every Saturday, Lina helped her father prepare soup at their small cafe. He had learned the recipe from his mother, and he measured most ingredients by eye. Lina admired his confidence, but she wanted to understand exactly how the dish was made. Her father agreed, although he warned her that the vegetables were not always the same size.

At first, Lina wrote down every spoonful and every minute. When she tried making the soup alone, she followed her notes carefully. However, it tasted weaker than her father's version. That extra liquid explained why the flavour had changed, even though she had used the same amount of seasoning.

Her father suggested tasting the soup at different stages instead of relying only on measurements. Lina began to notice how the smell and texture changed as it cooked. She still kept her notebook, but now it included descriptions as well as numbers.

One weekend, the supplier had only enough of the usual green vegetables for one small batch of soup. Lina suggested making a second batch with another kind from the market. Her father was unsure because regular customers expected a familiar dish. They served the two versions in small cups to a few customers and asked for their opinions.

The responses surprised them. Some customers preferred the familiar flavour, but others liked the new vegetables because they stayed firmer. Lina's father put both choices on the board, making it clear which ingredients each contained.

Lina later showed her grandmother the notebook. She expected her to dislike the changes to a family recipe. Instead, her grandmother laughed and explained that she had changed it herself many times when particular ingredients were difficult to find. The recipe Lina thought was fixed had already developed over many years.

Now Lina sees cooking differently. A recipe gives her a useful starting point, but she also needs to pay attention to the ingredients and the people who will eat the food. She wants to keep learning from her family while adding careful observations of her own. The notebook is no longer a set of rules she is afraid to break. It is a record of questions, experiments and discoveries that she can share with someone else one day.

FORM 3 · UNITS 1–2 · 09
Grammar Notes · Editable Text

Grammar Focus · Present Tenses and Nouns

Grammar notes are real, zoomable text, with Chinese support—not page screenshots.

Present Simple · 一般现在时

subject + base verb / -s

Habits, routines and facts（习惯、日常与事实）

My sister helps at home every day.

Present Continuous · 现在进行时

am / is / are + verb-ing

Happening now or temporary actions（正在发生或暂时情况）

She is helping Grandma this week.

State Verbs · 状态动词

know / like / understand / own

Usually not used in continuous forms（一般不用进行式）

I know the answer. NOT: I am knowing.

Countable & Uncountable · 可数与不可数

many / a few / fewer vs much / a little / less

Countable: a cousin / two cousins; Uncountable: rice / milk（米饭、牛奶）

a few biscuits; a little milk; fewer sandwiches; less milk
FORM 3 · UNITS 1–2 · 10
Grammar Notes · Editable Text

Grammar Focus · Past Tenses and Used To

Grammar notes are real, zoomable text, with Chinese support—not page screenshots.

Past Simple · 一般过去时

verb-ed / irregular past forms

Completed past actions（过去已完成的动作）

We cooked dinner yesterday.

Past Continuous · 过去进行时

was / were + verb-ing

An ongoing action at a past time（过去某刻正在进行）

I was cooking while Dad was washing the dishes.

Used to · 过去常常

used to + base verb

Past habits or states that are no longer true（过去的习惯或状态）

Grandma used to cook a large breakfast.

Would · 过去反复动作

would + base verb

Repeated past actions, not past states（过去反复发生的动作）

Every Sunday, Grandpa would take us to the market.
FORM 3 · UNITS 1–2 · 11
Grammar Notes · Editable Text

Grammar Focus · Be Used To / Get Used To

Be used to · 习惯于

be used to + noun / verb-ing

Already familiar with something（已经习惯）

She is used to preparing breakfast early.

Get used to · 逐渐习惯

get used to + noun / verb-ing

Becoming familiar（逐渐适应）

We are getting used to living together.
Remember： “used to + verb” = 过去常常；“be used to + -ing” = 已经习惯；“get used to + -ing” = 逐渐习惯。

Complete each question. Answers and English explanations are hidden until Review Answer is pressed.
11 When I was younger, I __________ (use) to dislike vegetables.
Review Answer
Answer: used
Used to describes a past state that is no longer true.
过去的状态不再持续，用 used to。
12 Every Sunday when we were children, Grandpa __________ take us to the market. (would / is used to)
Review Answer
Answer: would
Would describes a repeated past action here.
过去反复发生的动作可以使用 would。
13 Did your family __________ (use) to eat together every evening?
Review Answer
Answer: use
After did, use the base form.
did 后用原形 use。
14 My sister is used to __________ (cook) for herself.
Review Answer
Answer: cooking
Be used to is followed by a noun or an -ing form.
be used to 后接动词-ing。
15 It still feels strange, but I am getting used to __________ (share) a room with my cousin.
Review Answer
Answer: sharing
Get used to describes becoming familiar with something.
get used to 后接动词-ing，表示逐渐习惯。
16 My uncle __________ (own) a small cafe before he retired. Use the past simple or used to.
Review Answer
Answer: used to own / owned
A past state takes used to or the past simple, not habitual would.
过去状态可用 owned 或 used to own。
17 Rewrite using used to: We ate takeaway food regularly, but we do not do that now.
Review Answer
Answer: We used to eat takeaway food regularly.
Used to shows a past habit that has stopped.
used to 表示过去常常做，但现在不再这样。
18 Correct the error: She is knowing all the ingredients in this recipe.
Review Answer
Answer: She knows all the ingredients in this recipe.
Know is normally a state verb, so use the present simple.
know 是状态动词，通常用一般现在时。
19 Put the adjectives in the correct order. We saw a __________ serving dish at the market. (Turkish / beautiful / large)
Review Answer
Answer: beautiful large Turkish
Beautiful expresses opinion, large describes size and Turkish gives origin.
形容词顺序：看法 + 大小 + 来源。
20 Join using while: I was making the salad. My brother was laying the table.
Review Answer
Answer: While I was making the salad, my brother was laying the table.
While links two actions happening at the same time; reversed order is also accepted.
while 连接过去同时进行的两个动作。

1What will the family do together on Saturday afternoon?
Teacher Transcript
Ben: Are we still cycling by the lake after lunch? Ella: Dad says the path is flooded. He suggested the cinema instead, but Grandma is visiting and she cannot hear films clearly there. Ben: We should choose something she can enjoy too. Ella: I found a box of pictures from when she was young. We do not recognise half the people in them. Ben: Then let us spread them out on the dining table and ask her. We can go cycling another weekend.
Review Answer
Answer: B
The outdoor plan is cancelled and the cinema offer is declined. They will identify people in old photographs.
2Which dessert does Ben order?
Teacher Transcript
Ella: The meal includes dessert. Shall we share the chocolate cake? It comes with ice cream. Ben: I would rather have something lighter. Is there any fruit? Ella: Yes, but the menu says they serve it with yoghurt. Ben: I cannot have dairy products today. Ella: The waiter says they can leave that out. Ben: Perfect. I will have the fruit on its own, then.

Answer: C
Ben chooses fruit, then asks for it without yoghurt because he cannot have dairy.
3Where will Ella meet her brother?
Teacher Transcript
Ben: Your brother is waiting at the library, is he not? Ella: He was returning a book there. We had arranged to meet at the bus stop afterwards, but the road is closed. Ben: Where are you going instead? Ella: He is walking towards the shop with the striped awning, where Mum buys bread. Ben: Are you going inside for a snack? Ella: No, he said to wait outside. We are having lunch at home.

Answer: A
The brother will leave the library and meet her outside the bakery, not at the original bus stop.

Match Days to Problems · 6–10

Listening Part 2 · Family Cooking Week

Listen and match Tuesday–Saturday to A–H. Monday is the example: F. Tap a letter for instant feedback.
Teacher Transcript
Ella: How did your family cooking week go? You all cooked something different each day, did you not? Ben: Yes, from Monday to Saturday. On Monday, four of us tried to prepare dinner at once. We kept reaching across each other because the kitchen worktop was so small. Eventually, two of us moved to the dining table. Ella: What about Tuesday? Ben: We wanted to make fresh pesto. We had enough money and plenty of time, but the shop had sold its last bunch of basil. Dried herbs would not give us the same result, so we made a tomato sauce instead. Ella: Did you use the pesto recipe the next day? Ben: We planned to. Then Aunt May called to say she was joining us. She cannot eat nuts, and our sauce needed them. We chose a completely different sauce so everyone could share the meal. Ella: Sensible. What happened on Thursday? Ben: That was pizza day. The dough was ready and the topping looked lovely. Then we discovered the oven light came on but the oven stayed cold. Luckily, our neighbour let us use hers. The pizza was only a little late. Ella: And Friday? Ben: We made soup. Dad thought the recipe served two and doubled everything. It actually served six. Even after all five of us had eaten, there were several containers to freeze. At least it tasted good. Ella: Was Saturday easier? Ben: Not really. We tried a rice dish from an old recipe card. It said two hundred grams of rice, but did not say whether to weigh it before or after cooking. We had all the ingredients, but nobody agreed what that line meant. In the end, we phoned Grandma. Ella: I hope you wrote down her answer! Ben: We did. We want next time to be less confusing.
6. Tuesday
7. Wednesday
8. Thursday
9. Friday
10. Saturday
A. Someone could not eat an ingredient.
B. There was too little time to finish.
C. A piece of equipment stopped working.
D. The instructions were unclear.
E. An ingredient was unavailable.
F. There was not enough room to work.
G. The food was too expensive.
H. They made more food than they needed.

Listening MCQ · 11–15

Listening Part 3 · Community Cooking Event

Listen to Ella and Ben discussing a community cooking event. Select A, B or C, then review.
Teacher Transcript
Example 0 - Answer: C (Sunday) Ben: Is the community cooking event on Saturday? Ella: No, it is on Sunday. The poster went up on Friday, but the event is on Sunday. Questions 11-15 Ella: Have you seen the poster for Sunday's community cooking event, Ben? I am thinking of entering. Ben: I thought you could already make the vegetable parcels they are teaching. Ella: I can. Grandma showed me last year. The recipe is not the reason I want to go. I usually work with the same friends at school, and I would like to get better at doing a task with people I do not already know. Ben: You will get a certificate too, will you not? Ella: Only the volunteers get those, not the cooking teams. Did you notice the new team rule? The first poster said we could bring our own team, but they have changed that. Ben: Do we have to bring an adult now? Ella: No. The organisers put the teams together. If you arrive with a friend or relative, they place you in different groups. They want neighbours to get to know one another. Ben: That might be awkward at first, but it makes sense. How will they choose the winning dish? Do we have to make it look exactly like the chef's? Ella: Actually, they encourage our own ideas. Presentation counts for a few marks, but the largest share is for using the ingredients sensibly and leaving as little as possible in the rubbish bin. Ben: I like that. I would rather use the whole carrot than cut most of it away to make a perfect shape. Do we need to bring knives or bowls? Ella: Everything is supplied. But the parcels have egg in the pastry, and you do not eat eggs. The poster does not mention alternatives. Ben: I will message the organiser tonight and ask if there is a version I can make. We should know before paying the entry fee. Ella: Good. How about getting home? The event finishes at half past three, but the bus stop near the market is closed that day. Ben: My sister could collect us, except that she starts work at three. Could your dad help? Ella: He can come at four, not before. That would mean waiting for half an hour. Ben: That is fine. We can help clear the tables while we wait. Let us arrange that rather than hunt for another bus stop.
11Why does Ella want to take part?
A. To practise working with someone outside her usual circle.
B. To learn a recipe that her family has never tried.
C. To earn a certificate for her school application.
Review Answer
Answer: A
Her aim is to work with unfamiliar people, rather than gain a certificate or a new family recipe.
12Suppose Ella, Ben and Ella’s cousin arrive together. Which arrangement follows the new team rule?
A. Ella and Ben join one group; her cousin joins another.
B. Ella, Ben and her cousin each join a different group.
C. Ella and her cousin join one group; Ben joins another.
Review Answer
Answer: B
The rule separates participants from friends or relatives they arrive with.
13What matters most when the dishes are judged?
A. How closely they copy the demonstration dish.
B. How attractively they are arranged on the plate.
C. How well the ingredients are used without waste.
Review Answer
Answer: C
The biggest share of marks is for using ingredients sensibly and wasting little.
14What does Ben agree to ask the organiser?
A. Whether the organisers will provide the cooking tools he needs.
B. Whether he can prepare a version that suits his diet.
C. Whether he is allowed to bring suitable ingredients from home.
Review Answer
Answer: B
Ben cannot eat eggs and agrees to ask whether a suitable version is available.
15How will they travel home?
A. With Ella’s father, if they can wait until four.
B. On the bus from the stop by the market.
C. With Ben’s sister immediately after the event.
Review Answer
Answer: A
They accept the father’s later lift and will help tidy up while waiting.

Listening Part 4 · Workshop Booking

Listen twice and complete each blank with no more than three words and/or a number. Review answers individually.
Teacher Transcript
Assistant: Green Kitchen workshops. How can I help? Ben: I would like to confirm our family booking for Sunday, please. It is under the name Ben Lim. Assistant: Certainly. I have twelve people written down. Ben: That is the number of guests. I forgot to include myself and my sister. We will both take part as well. Assistant: So fourteen altogether. That is still within our limit of sixteen. Has everyone agreed to the usual price of forty ringgit each? Ben: Yes, although your website mentioned a group discount. Assistant: That is right. For groups of at least ten, we take five ringgit off the usual price for each person. Ben: So thirty-five each. Does that include the ingredients? Assistant: Yes, and drinks. There is nothing else to pay unless you buy something from the shop afterwards. Ben: My aunt thinks the workshop starts at ten. Is that correct? Assistant: Please arrive at ten so we can check everyone in. The cooking itself starts at a quarter past ten. It ends at twelve fifteen, and you can stay to eat until one. Ben: Fine. What should everyone bring? Do we need our own knives? Assistant: No, we provide those, and containers for anything you want to take home. Everyone does need an apron, though. Wear clothes that you do not mind getting a little dirty. Ben: I will tell them. Shall we meet you at the front entrance? Assistant: Normally, yes, but some repair work is taking place there. Meet at the side entrance instead. There is a clear sign from the car park. Do not go round to the delivery door at the back. Ben: Side entrance. Got it. Thank you.

Answer: 14 / fourteen
Twelve guests plus Ben and his sister make fourteen.
17 Cost per person (RM)
Review Answer
Answer: 35 / thirty-five
The group discount reduces forty ringgit by five.
18 Workshop begins at
Review Answer
Answer: 10.15 a.m. / 10:15 / quarter past ten
Ten o’clock is the arrival time; cooking begins fifteen minutes later.
19 Each person should bring an
Review Answer

Knives and containers are supplied; everyone brings an apron.
20 Meeting point

Listening Information Transfer

Listening Part 5 · Family Recipe Exhibition

Listen twice and complete each blank with no more than three words and/or a number. Review answers individually.
Teacher Transcript
Ella: Before you leave, here are the final arrangements for our Family Recipe Exhibition in March. Each student should choose a recipe that matters to someone in their family. It need not be unusual or expensive. We are interested in the story behind it. The original deadline was the tenth of March. Several classes will be away that day, so you now have two extra days. Please hand everything in by the twelfth of March, not on the exhibition day itself. For the written story, about eighty words will usually be enough. You may write more if you need to, but do not go over one hundred and twenty words. The recipe instructions do not count towards that limit. You should also provide one photograph of the finished dish. Some students asked whether a picture of the person cooking would be better. You may add one if you wish, but it does not replace the photograph of the completed food. Please do not bring the food itself; we cannot keep it fresh throughout the exhibition. We originally planned to use the library, but more families have said they are coming than we expected. The exhibition will therefore take place in the school hall. The classrooms will still be used for normal lessons. Finally, visitors will be able to respond to your work. Instead of writing comments on paper, they can record a short voice message using a tablet beside each display. They might share a memory or explain why a recipe interests them. We will collect those recordings for you afterwards. I am looking forward to hearing the stories your families have to tell.
21 Final day to hand in entries
Review Answer
Answer: 12 March / 12th March / March 12
The original deadline of 10 March moved two days later.
22 Maximum number of words
Review Answer
Answer: 120
Eighty words is suggested; 120 is the maximum.
23 Bring one photograph of the
Review Answer
Answer: finished dish / completed food
The photograph must show the completed dish.
24 New exhibition venue
Review Answer
Answer: school hall / hall
The hall replaces the library because more space is needed.
25 Format of visitors’ feedback
Review Answer
Answer: voice message / audio message / audio recording
Visitors leave recorded messages rather than paper comments.
